title: Zero External Dependencies
content:
This proof uses **no imports whatsoever** - not even Mathlib. It relies only on Lean's built-in types (`Nat`, `Bool`) and core tactics.

This demonstrates that the halting problem's undecidability is a purely logical result, requiring no sophisticated mathematical machinery.
mathContext:
The proof needs only:
- Natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (for program codes)
- Booleans $\{\text{true}, \text{false}\}$ (for halt/loop)
- Boolean negation $\neg$
prerequisites: Lean 4 import system and module structure
Lean built-in types: Nat, Bool
Distinction between core language and library dependencies

title: Halting Oracle
content:
A **halting oracle** is a hypothetical function that takes two natural numbers — a program code $p$ and an input $i$ — and returns whether program $p$ halts on input $i$.

We model programs as natural numbers via **Gödel numbering**: every finite syntactic object can be encoded as a natural number, making `Nat → Nat → Bool` a faithful abstraction. The claim is that no total computable function can serve as a correct halting oracle.
prerequisites: Turing machine model of computation (1936)
Decision problems and yes/no questions about programs
Function types in Lean: Nat → Nat → Bool
Gödel numbering: encoding programs as natural numbers

title: Program Behavior
content:
A **behavior** is a function from inputs to booleans, representing whether a program halts on each possible input.

Every program has a behavior (even if we can't compute it). The diagonal construction will create a behavior that no oracle can correctly predict.
mathContext:
$b : \mathbb{N} \to \{\text{true}, \text{false}\}$

$b(n) = \text{true}$ means the program halts on input $n$
prerequisites: Extensional equality of functions (same behavior on all inputs)
Higher-order functions and function types
Semantics of programs as input-output mappings

title: The Diagonal Behavior
content:
The **diagonal behavior** is the key construction. Given an oracle $H$:

1. For input $n$, ask the oracle: "Does program $n$ halt on input $n$?"
2. Return the **opposite** of what the oracle says

This creates a behavior that deliberately contradicts the oracle's self-referential predictions. In Lean this is just `fun n => !(H n n)` — three tokens that encode the entire impossibility argument.
mathContext:
$\text{diagonal}(H)(n) = \neg H(n, n)$

If $H$ says program $n$ halts on itself, diagonal loops.
If $H$ says program $n$ loops on itself, diagonal halts.
prerequisites: Boolean negation: ¬true = false, ¬false = true
Self-application: applying a function to its own encoding
Cantor's diagonal argument (1891) — the prototype for this construction

title: Self-Reference Plus Negation
content:
The undecidability arises from combining two elements:

1. **Self-reference**: We ask about program $n$ running on input $n$
2. **Negation**: We do the opposite of what the oracle predicts

This same pattern appears in Cantor's diagonal argument, Godel's incompleteness, and Russell's paradox.
mathContext:
The **liar-paradox** structure:
"This program does the opposite of what you predict."

No prediction can be correct! The diagonal argument is a general method:
- Cantor (1891): diagonal real differs from every $f(n)$, so no surjection $\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}$
- Gödel (1931): diagonal sentence $G$ encodes "$G$ is unprovable"; if provable, false; if true, unprovable
- Turing (1936): diagonal program $D$ does $\neg H(D,D)$; if $H$ correct, contradiction

All share: construct an object that **refers to itself** and **negates the prediction**.
prerequisites: Fixed-point theorems (Kleene's recursion theorem is the positive dual)
Gödel's incompleteness theorem — same self-referential structure
Cantor's diagonalization for uncountability of ℝ
Russell's paradox: the set R = {x : x ∉ x}

title: Diagonal Differs from Oracle
content:
**Key Lemma**: The diagonal behavior always differs from the oracle's prediction at self-application points.

For any program code $n$:
$\text{diagonal}(H)(n) \neq H(n, n)$

This follows immediately from the fact that $\neg b \neq b$ for any boolean.
mathContext:
$	ext{diagonal}(H)(n) = 
eg H(n, n) 
eq H(n, n)$

Because $
eg 	ext{true} = 	ext{false} 
eq 	ext{true}$
and $
eg 	ext{false} = 	ext{true} 
eq 	ext{false}$
prerequisites: Boolean case analysis (cases on Bool values)
Lean's simp tactic and Boolean simplification lemmas
Proof by contradiction (intro h; cases; derive False)

title: No Correct Halting Oracle Exists
content:
**Main Theorem**: For any oracle $H$ and any code $c$ that implements the diagonal behavior, the oracle $H$ cannot correctly predict $c$'s behavior on input $c$.

If the oracle were correct, then:
- $H(c, c) = \text{true}$ would mean $c$ halts on $c$
- But $c$ implements diagonal, so $c(c) = \neg H(c,c) = \text{false}$

Contradiction! (And similarly for the false case.)
mathContext:
$\forall H, \forall c,$ if $c$ implements $\text{diagonal}(H)$, then
$H(c, c) = \text{true} \Rightarrow c(c) = \text{false}$ (contradiction)
$H(c, c) = \text{false} \Rightarrow c(c) = \text{true}$ (contradiction)
prerequisites: Universal quantification and proof by contradiction in Lean
Implication hypotheses (h_halts, h_loops) in Lean tactic mode
Boolean case analysis: cases h : H c c with | true => ... | false => ...

title: Case: Oracle Says Halt
content:
**Case 1**: Suppose $H(c, c) = \text{true}$ (oracle predicts halt).

Then by definition of diagonal:
$\text{diagonal}(H)(c) = \neg H(c, c) = \text{false}$

But the hypothesis says $c$ correctly implements diagonal, so $c$ halting means diagonal returns true.

Contradiction: $\text{false} = \text{true}$.
prerequisites: Lean's cases tactic for exhaustive Bool case analysis
simp tactic with named hypotheses (simp [hc] at h)
Proof by contradiction: deriving False from a hypothesis

title: Case: Oracle Says Loop
content:
**Case 2**: Suppose $H(c, c) = \text{false}$ (oracle predicts loop).

Then by definition of diagonal:
$\text{diagonal}(H)(c) = \neg H(c, c) = \text{true}$

But the hypothesis says $c$ correctly implements diagonal, so diagonal returning true means $c$ halts.

Contradiction: $H$ said $c$ loops but $c$ halts.
prerequisites: Lean's cases tactic for exhaustive Bool case analysis
Symmetry of the contradiction: both Bool cases are forced
simp tactic normalizing Boolean expressions

title: Logical Equivalence Formulation
content:
A cleaner restatement: there is no oracle-code pair $(H, c)$ where the oracle's prediction matches the diagonal behavior in both directions.

The biconditional $H(c,c) = \text{true} \iff \text{diagonal}(H)(c) = \text{true}$ cannot hold, because the diagonal is defined to be the negation.
prerequisites: Logical biconditional (↔) and its use in Lean
Negation of a conjunction (¬(P ∧ Q))
Equivalence of different formulations of the same undecidability result

title: No Self-Halting Decider
content:
**Alternative Formulation**: No function can correctly determine its own halting behavior on its own encoding.

For any proposed decider $H : \mathbb{N} \to \text{Bool}$ (where $H(n)$ means "program $n$ halts on $n$"), there exists a behavior that $H$ gets wrong everywhere.
prerequisites: Existential statements (∃ b, ...) and witness construction in Lean
refine and exact tactics for providing witnesses
Diagonal argument: the witness is the negation function b(n) = ¬H(n)

title: Halting Problem Undecidable
content:
**Final Summary**: For any halting oracle $H$, the diagonal program provides an explicit counterexample.

The diagonal behavior exists (we constructed it), and it differs from every oracle prediction at the self-application point. Therefore no oracle can be correct.
prerequisites: Combining prior lemmas (diagonal_differs) in a final proof
Existential witnesses: explicit counterexample via diagonalBehavior
Lean's exact tactic for closing goals with a term

title: Connections to Other Results
content:
The diagonal technique appears across mathematics and logic:

- **Cantor** (1891): No surjection $\mathbb{N} \to 2^{\mathbb{N}}$ - same construction!
- **Godel** (1931): No complete consistent theory - "this statement is unprovable"
- **Russell** (1901): No set of all sets - the set of sets not containing themselves
- **Tarski** (1936): Truth is undefinable - "this statement is false"
mathContext:
All share the pattern: **self-reference + negation = impossibility**

| Result | Self-referential object | Negation mechanism |
|--------|------------------------|--------------------|
| Cantor | Diagonal real $d_n = 1 - f(n)_n$ | $d$ differs from $f(n)$ at position $n$ |
| Russell | Set $R = \{x : x\notin x\}$ | Membership negated |
| Gödel | Sentence $G = $ "$G$ is unprovable" | Provability negated |
| Tarski | Sentence $L = $ "$L$ is false" | Truth negated |
| Turing | Program $D(n) = \neg H(n,n)$ | Halting negated |
prerequisites: Cantor's theorem: |A| < |P(A)| and its diagonal proof
Gödel's incompleteness theorems (1931)
Russell's paradox and naive set theory
Tarski's undefinability of truth theorem (1936)

title: Visualizing the Diagonal
content:
Imagine an infinite table where row $n$ shows whether program $n$ halts on each input.

The diagonal consists of the self-application entries: does program 0 halt on 0? Does program 1 halt on 1? Etc.

Flipping each diagonal entry gives a behavior that differs from every row at the critical position. If this flipped diagonal could be program $d$, then row $d$ would have to differ from itself at column $d$ - impossible!
mathContext:
```
       Input 0  Input 1  Input 2  Input 3  ...
Prog 0:  [halt]  loop     halt     loop    ...
Prog 1:  loop    [halt]   halt     loop    ...
Prog 2:  halt    halt     [loop]   halt    ...
Prog 3:  loop    loop     halt     [halt]  ...
  ...
Diag:   halt     halt     loop     halt   ...  (diagonal entries)
Flipped: loop    loop     halt     loop   ...  (the counterexample)
```
The flipped diagonal agrees with **no row**: it differs from row $n$ at column $n$ by construction. If flipped diagonal were program $d$, row $d$ must differ from itself at column $d$ — impossible.
prerequisites: Matrix representation of program behaviors (programs × inputs)
Cantor's original diagonal argument for uncountability of [0,1]
Self-application: the diagonal entry (n, n) is the key position

title: Practical Implications
content:
The halting problem's undecidability has real-world consequences:

1. **Static Analysis**: No tool can detect all infinite loops or bugs; any sound analyser must be incomplete
2. **Compilers**: Can't always optimize away dead code — reachability is undecidable in general
3. **Verification**: Fully automatic program verification is impossible; interactive provers require human guidance
4. **Security**: Can't perfectly detect all malware behaviors — virus scanners operate under fundamental limits
5. **Type Checking**: Termination checking for dependent type theories faces the same barrier

Every static analysis tool must either miss some problems (unsound) or report false positives (incomplete).
mathContext: Rice's Theorem generalizes this: ANY non-trivial semantic property of programs is undecidable.
prerequisites: Rice's theorem: any non-trivial semantic property of programs is undecidable
The theory of program verification and static analysis
Reduction between undecidable problems (halting ≤ₘ any non-trivial semantic property)
